title: PlayIQ: Sports Analytics Dashboard
description: A sports analytics dashboard for MLB, NBA, WNBA, NFL, NHL, and NCAAB, with matchup, form, roster, and modeling tabs for each game. The projections use Log5 batter-vs-pitcher matchups, Binomial and Poisson distributions, and additive scoring, and every number shows its data source, inputs, and formula. An XGBoost model for MLB first-five-innings outcomes is trained offline in a GitHub Actions workflow, and the Claude API adds written game analysis.

insights.summary: A sports analytics dashboard with no build step: React 18 and Babel Standalone load from a CDN, and the backend uses only Node's built-in http/https modules, with no npm dependencies. Apart from one XGBoost model, every projection is plain arithmetic, and each one shows where its number came from.
highlights: Badged each day's games as HOT PLAY, LEAN, LOOK, or FADE so the strongest matchups show up first
Built an Edge Finder that uses Log5 matchup math to project per-player thresholds for MLB, NBA, and WNBA
Built a live MLB feed with the scoreboard, base runners, pitch locations, and play-by-play, refreshed at most every 10 seconds
Added live MLB and NFL feeds with win probability, an NFL field and stadium view, and an NFL Edge Finder based on last-5 and career-vs-opponent splits
Moved model training into a GitHub Actions workflow, so the first-five-innings model retrains without touching the live site
Gave every non-ML score a "why" note naming its API endpoint, inputs, and formula

artifacts.alt: PlayIQ dashboard: sport selection with live data indicators

title: Chroma: U-Fund Crowdfunding Platform
description: A charity crowdfunding site built by a team of four. Donors browse funding needs, group them into bundles, check out from a cart, and set up recurring subscriptions. The back end is a Spring Boot REST API split into controller, model, and DAO layers with file-based storage, and the Angular front end covers login, the dashboard, search, detail pages, and checkout. A JUnit suite tests all three back-end layers.

insights.summary: A four-person Agile team project. Angular components call a Spring Boot REST API, requests go through controllers to a DAO layer, and because each DAO sits behind an interface, storage can be swapped without changing the controllers. JUnit tests cover the controller, model, and persistence layers.
highlights: Designed five resources (needs, bundles, shopping cart, subscriptions, and users), each with its own controller, model, and DAO
Built 15 Angular components covering login and registration, the dashboard, needs and subscription search, detail views, and checkout
Put each DAO behind an interface, so the file-based storage can be replaced without changing the controllers
Wrote JUnit tests for the controller, model, and persistence layers
Configured CORS and environment-specific API endpoints for local development

title: ACL Unplanned Surgery Predictive Model
description: A research project at the University of Pittsburgh's AIBIDS program on predicting which ACL reconstruction (ACLR) patients will need an unplanned surgery afterward. I pulled pre-surgery clinical notes from a UPMC database of de-identified patients (2013-2021) with SQL, used an LLM to classify activity level from the notes, and evaluated activity level as a predictor alongside social determinants of health (SDoH) in logistic regression models.

artifacts.alt: Research poster: Enhancing Prediction of Unplanned Surgeries After ACL Reconstruction: Evaluating the Role of Activity Level Among SDoH Factors

highlights: Surfaced risk patterns in 5,000+ de-identified patient records to inform the predictive model
Extracted 464 pre-surgery clinical notes using SQL CTEs, joins, and embeddings
Classified activity levels with DeepSeek-R1 14B, reaching 0.89 F1 on elite athletes with 6 batches of hand-annotated examples
Built logistic regression models in scikit-learn to predict unplanned surgery from SDoH factors
Presented a research poster on activity level as an SDoH predictor to faculty, peers, and stakeholders

title: Stock Dip Analysis API
description: A TypeScript and Express API that scores whether a well-known stock's dip is worth a closer look. It pulls quotes, candles, and company news from Finnhub, falls back to Alpha Vantage for candles, and computes RSI itself when the provider's indicator endpoint isn't available. A 100-point rule-based score weighs dip depth against the 50-day moving average, RSI, and news sentiment, then labels the stock GOOD DIP, WATCH, or AVOID.

insights.summary: A stock screening API that flags dips worth researching. It doesn't try to model valuation, fundamentals, or analyst ratings. The scoring rules are fixed and documented, so every label traces back to the four inputs behind it.
highlights: Scored stocks out of 100: dip depth (30), price above the 50-day SMA (25), RSI below 35 (20), and no bad-news keywords (25)
Fell back to Alpha Vantage for historical candles when Finnhub blocks that endpoint on free-tier keys
Calculated RSI from candle closing prices instead of relying on a provider's indicator endpoint
Added a response cache and a normalizing layer so third-party rate limits don't break scoring
Ran the service and a seeded PostgreSQL database together with Docker Compose

title: Movie Database Management System
description: A PostgreSQL movie database and Python application built with a team of five. An ETL pipeline cleans Kaggle datasets and loads them into a normalized schema, and the app connects to the remote database server over an SSH tunnel.

insights.summary: A five-person database project. Raw Kaggle CSVs are cleaned and loaded into a normalized PostgreSQL schema, and a Python app with auth, user, movie, and collection modules runs queries against it.
highlights: Designed a normalized schema that supports search and queries like top-rated films, genre breakdowns, and actor co-appearances
Built an ETL pipeline that cleans Kaggle CSV datasets before loading them
Organized the app into auth, user, movie, and collection modules over a shared connection layer
Used SSH tunneling for secure remote access to the database server
Documented both Docker and manual setup so the project runs locally either way

title: Secure Distributed Messenger
description: A peer-to-peer encrypted chat app in C#, built with a team of four, where every node is both a server and a client in a TCP mesh. I owned peer discovery and reconnection: UDP broadcasts every 5 seconds, dropping peers that go quiet for 30 seconds, a heartbeat check that flags a connection after 15 seconds of silence, and exponential-backoff reconnects. Each message is encrypted with AES-256 using a per-peer session key exchanged over RSA-2048, and signed with RSA-SHA256.

insights.summary: An end-to-end encrypted console messenger with no central server, built for CSCI 251 (Parallel and Distributed Systems) over three sprints. Each node runs parallel accept, receive, heartbeat, discovery, and timeout loops, and messages are sent as length-prefixed JSON over full-duplex TCP.
highlights: Implemented UDP peer discovery broadcasting PEER:{id}:{port} on port 5001, then connecting and exchanging keys with each new peer over TCP
Prevented duplicate connections when two peers connect at once by letting only the peer with the smaller ID start the connection
Detected failures two ways: a 15-second heartbeat timeout and a 30-second discovery timeout
Added exponential-backoff reconnection (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s, capped at 30 s, five attempts)
Secured traffic with an RSA-OAEP-wrapped AES-256-CBC session key per peer and RSA-SHA256 message signatures

title: ASL Calculator
description: A calculator, built with a teammate, that reads American Sign Language numbers and operators from a webcam and evaluates the expression when you sign Done. I built the vision side: MediaPipe tracking for two hands with separate smoothing for each, and a feature extractor that normalizes the 21 hand landmarks for position and scale and detects which fingers are extended. A Random Forest classifier uses those features to recognize digits in real time.

insights.summary: A gesture calculator built with a teammate. Recognition runs in three steps: landmark tracking, feature extraction, and classification. A state machine walks through number, operator, number until it sees the Done sign.
highlights: Tracked up to two hands at once with per-hand exponential smoothing to steady landmarks between frames
Normalized landmarks to the wrist and hand size so features stay stable as the hand moves or changes distance
Improved thumb detection to account for its shorter length and sideways motion
Combined a 42-dimensional landmark vector with 5 finger-extension states for the classifier input
Built data-collection, training and live-classification tools for digits 0 to 9

title: Race Condition Detective
description: Found and fixed race conditions in five intentionally broken C# components: a bank ledger, a counter, a cache, a logger, and a queue. Each bug came down to a non-atomic read-modify-write on shared state, and each got the smallest fix that made it correct instead of one big lock. Every bug is written up with where it is, the thread interleaving that triggers it, the fix, and why the fix works.

insights.summary: A concurrency debugging assignment. The same lesson kept coming up: lines that look like one step, like _count++ or assigning a new balance, are really a read, a change, and a write, and two threads can interleave them and lose an update.
highlights: Verified every fix against a randomized harness: 10/10 trials passing on all five components, 15/15 points
Found lost updates in the bank's deposit and withdraw methods caused by non-atomic updates to the shared balance
Replaced _count++ with Interlocked.Increment, which makes the increment atomic without a full lock
Used locks where a critical section spans several operations, and Interlocked operations where only one value changes
Wrote up every bug: location, shared state, why it fails, the fix, and why the fix holds

artifacts.alt: Race Condition Detective verification harness, all five components fixed

title: Wildfire Simulation
description: A wildfire simulation in C where fire spreads probabilistically across a grid of trees. Whether a tree catches fire depends on its burning neighbors, the forest density, and a burn probability, and trees are placed with a Fisher-Yates shuffle.

artifacts.alt: Wildfire simulation output showing fire spreading across the forest grid

insights.summary: A grid-based fire spread simulation in C. Every parameter (grid size, tree density, catch probability, initial burn proportion, and the neighbor threshold for ignition) is set on the command line, so different fire conditions are easy to compare. It compiles cleanly with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic.
highlights: Implemented probabilistic spread where ignition depends on the share of burning neighbors against a configurable threshold
Built two display modes: an overlay mode that redraws in place and a print mode that outputs N time steps
Tracked per-cycle and total state changes to detect when the fire stops spreading
Used a Fisher-Yates shuffle for unbiased random placement of trees across the grid
Separated the simulation from the display code into modules built with a Makefile

title: Pathfinding Search Algorithms
description: BFS, DFS, and A* search in Java, compared on a road network of US state capitals loaded from city and edge data files. A* uses straight-line distance between coordinates as its heuristic, and all three algorithms share one graph so they run on identical routes.

insights.summary: Three classic search algorithms on the same weighted graph. From Olympia to Tallahassee, A* and BFS both take 8 hops, but A*'s route is 1,055 miles shorter. DFS takes 19 hops and 8,292 miles.
highlights: Measured on Olympia to Tallahassee: A* 8 hops / 4,751 mi, BFS 8 hops / 5,806 mi, DFS 19 hops / 8,292 mi
Implemented A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic over geographic city coordinates
Loaded the road network from separate city and edge data files into a shared graph structure
Gave BFS, DFS, and A* a common search interface so they run on identical inputs

artifacts.alt: BFS vs A* route comparison from Olympia to Tallahassee

title: Astros and Hoppers
description: Two Java puzzle games, Hoppers and Astros, built with a partner for RIT's Computer Science II course. Hoppers is a frog-jumping puzzle, and in Astros you move explorers to guide an astronaut home. Both use a shared breadth-first search solver to find the shortest solution, and both can be played in a JavaFX window or as a text interface.

highlights: Built each game with a model that notifies both a JavaFX GUI and a text interface through the Observer pattern
Solved puzzles with a shared breadth-first search that returns the shortest sequence of moves
Added hint, load, select, and reset commands so players can step through a puzzle or load a new one from a file

title: Evolutionary Stable Strategy Simulation
description: A Hawk-Dove simulation in Python that shows how an evolutionarily stable strategy emerges from simple encounter rules. Hawks and doves compete over a fixed resource, and aggression has a survival cost for hawks. A menu lets you step through single encounters or run 1,000 to 10,000 at once, and population size, hawk percentage, resource amount, and hawk cost are all command-line options.

insights.summary: A simulation of the classic Hawk-Dove game. The main result: the stable mix of strategies depends on the hawk cost compared with the resource value, not on how many hawks there are at the start. When the cost is higher than the resource, hawks die out no matter how many there were.
highlights: Verified the core ESS result at runtime: with resource 50 and hawk cost 100, hawk-hawk encounters kill both hawks while dove pairs split +25 each
Modeled hawk-hawk, hawk-dove, and dove-dove encounters with different payoffs and survival outcomes
Showed that hawk cost relative to the resource drives the equilibrium more than the starting hawk percentage
Made every simulation variable a command-line argument with defaults, so runs are reproducible
Split the code into individual, simulation, and entry-point modules

artifacts.alt: Hawk-Dove simulation output showing hawk-hawk mutual elimination

title: Reaction Timing Racing Game
description: A multiplayer Roblox racing game where you move forward on a ten-line track by tapping in time after a random flash. The server runs the game loop (intermission, countdown, flash timing, and win detection), and a client script handles input and feedback. All tuning values, from flash windows and cooldowns to track layout and game pass IDs, live in one shared config module.

insights.summary: A server-authoritative multiplayer game written outside Roblox Studio. Rojo syncs the project files into the engine, so the code lives in Git like any other repository, and balance changes are one-line edits to the config module.
highlights: Built a server-authoritative loop covering intermission, countdown, randomized flash timing, and win detection
Split the code across ServerScriptService, StarterPlayerScripts, and a shared ReplicatedStorage module
Randomized flash intervals within a tuned range so players cannot memorize the timing
Designed game pass abilities (Reflex Boost extends the tap window; Eliminator has a cooldown) around the timing mechanic
Used Rojo and Aftman to keep the project in version control instead of inside Roblox Studio

title: Postfix Expression Interpreter
description: An interpreter in C that reads postfix expressions, builds an expression tree, evaluates it, and prints the infix form. It uses a linked-list stack, a symbol table loaded from a file for named variables, and tree nodes for arithmetic, modulo, conditional, and assignment operators. It reports parse and evaluation errors and runs without memory leaks.

insights.summary: A read-eval-print loop over postfix input, built from hand-written data structures with manual memory management.
highlights: Parsed postfix tokens into an expression tree using a dynamically allocated linked-list stack
Supported +, -, *, /, %, the ? conditional and = assignment into a file-backed symbol table
Reported distinct parse and evaluation errors such as too few tokens, unknown symbols and division by zero
Tracked down and fixed memory leaks across stack, tree and symbol-table code

title: Decision Cascade Classifier
description: A decision-cascade classifier written from scratch in Python and R that separates two classes using two numeric features. The tree builder tries every threshold on each feature, scores splits with a cost function that balances node size against purity, and writes the trained model out as a standalone Python classify() function. I tuned the purity weight for the best accuracy and plotted the decision boundaries.

insights.summary: A CSCI 420 (Data Mining) project. Training outputs a nested if/else classifier that runs without the training program.
highlights: Implemented exhaustive threshold search over both features at every node
Designed a cost function that rewards pure nodes and stops the tree from creating tiny splits
Generated a standalone classify(HemHt, BowTieWd) function from the trained tree
Visualized training points against every learned threshold boundary

title: PCA and K-Means Customer Segmentation
description: Segmented shopping-cart data across 20 product categories by computing the covariance matrix and its eigendecomposition by hand to perform PCA. Chose the number of components from a cumulative explained-variance plot, projected the data onto the top two principal components, and ran K-Means in that space. Mapped the cluster centers back to the original 20 categories to describe what each customer segment buys.

insights.summary: A two-person CSCI 420 project combining hand-built PCA with K-Means clustering to find customer segments.
highlights: Computed covariance, eigenvalues and eigenvectors with NumPy instead of a library PCA call
Plotted cumulative explained variance to justify how many components to keep
Clustered the 2-D projection with K-Means and mapped the centers back to original categories

artifacts.alt: K-Means clusters (k=4) on the PCA projection

title: One-Rule Threshold Classifier
description: Built a one-rule classifier in R that flags aggressive drivers from traffic-station data. Swept every threshold on speed, lane-change count and brightness, scored each by false-positive and false-negative rates, and chose the single feature and threshold with the lowest error. Exported the winning rule as a standalone classifier script that runs on new test files.

insights.summary: A CSCI 420 project comparing single-feature decision rules on combined multi-station traffic data.
highlights: Combined dozens of per-station CSV files into one dataset
Evaluated false-positive and false-negative rates at every candidate threshold
Picked lane changes with a threshold of 2 as the lowest-error rule and saved it as a reusable script
